name: Chandragupta Maurya
info: Chandragupta Maurya, who reigned from about 320 to about 298 BCE, founded the Maurya Empire in Magadha after defeating the Nanda dynasty, and took control of the eastern Indus Valley after Alexander the Great's campaign.

facts.born: Year and place unknown; there are no historical facts about his origins and early life, only legends. The year given here, c. 320 BCE, is the conventional start of his reign. Greek and Roman, Hindu, Buddhist and Jain sources give differing accounts of his family
facts.died: Date, place and circumstances unclear and disputed; according to Roy, he abdicated c. 298 BCE and died between 297 and 293 BCE. Digambara Jain tradition says he fasted to death at Shravanabelagola in Karnataka, a story that Sushma Jansari calls late and problematic
facts.role: Founder and first emperor of the Maurya Empire, based in Magadha; reigned c. 320 BCE – c. 298 BCE (scholars give dates from 324 or 322 to 297 or 293 BCE)
facts.known: overthrowing the Nanda dynasty and founding the Maurya Empire; the war against Alexander's Greek governors in the Indus Valley; the marriage alliance and exchange of 500 elephants with Seleucus I Nicator; a decentralised administration with provinces and a council of advisers; irrigation works and roads; his partnership with Chanakya in the legends; the Jain story of his renunciation

t: Chandragupta rose in the unrest that followed Alexander the Great's Indian campaign, defeated the Nanda dynasty in Magadha and founded the Maurya Empire, though the order and dates of these events remain debated.

He made a dynastic marriage alliance with Seleucus I Nicator c. 305–303 BCE, receiving the regions along the Indus and sending 500 elephants in exchange, and ruled through a decentralised administration of provinces and local governments.

His life reaches us only through Greek and Roman fragments and Hindu, Buddhist and Jain texts written centuries later, which disagree on his origins, his rise and his death, so historians treat most of the narrative with caution.
dyk: Sir William Jones proposed in 1793 that the Indian king "Sandracottus" of the Greek and Roman writers was Chandragupta of the Sanskrit texts, which made it possible to match Indian and Graeco-Roman history; his reign has been called "the sheet anchor of Indian chronology".
ev: Alexander the Great ends his Indian campaign in 326 to 325 BCE; Plutarch later claims that Chandragupta, as a young man, saw him
Alexander dies in Babylon and war breaks out between his generals, leaving unrest in the Indian territories he had assigned to Greek governors
Chandragupta's conquest of Magadha and the defeat of the Nandas is generally dated between 322 and 319 BCE, though a later chronology places it c. 311–305 BCE
Jansari dates Chandragupta's arrival in the Punjab here, in line with the chronology of Greek history
Chandragupta and Seleucus I Nicator confront each other and then, by about 303 BCE, form a dynastic marriage alliance
According to Roy, Chandragupta's abdication may be dated here
According to Roy, Chandragupta dies at some point between 297 and 293 BCE

sections.early:
There are no historical facts about Chandragupta's origins and early life, only legends, and the narrative of his reign is deduced mainly from a few fragments in Greek and Roman sources and a few Indian religious texts, all written centuries after his death. None of the ancient texts says when he was born. Plutarch claimed that he saw Alexander the Great as a young man during Alexander's invasion of India, c. 326–325 BCE, and on that assumption Raychaudhuri proposed in 1923 that he may have been born after 350 BCE.

The sources differ on his family. The Roman historian Justin, in the 2nd century CE, says he was of humble origin. Some Hindu texts make him a son of one of the Nanda king's wives, named Mura, or of a concubine; the 11th-century Kashmiri texts, the Kathasaritsagara and the Brihat-Katha-Manjari, make him a son of Purva-Nanda. The Sanskrit play Mudrarakshasa calls him Vrishala, a word that can mean the son of a shudra or the best of kings; Radha Kumud Mukherjee argued for the second sense. Buddhist texts such as the Mahavamsa, written about seven centuries after his dynasty ended, describe him as a Kshatriya of the Moriya clan, a branch of the Buddha's Shakya family, and explain the name Maurya by peacocks (mora in Pali). These sources seek to link the dynasty of Ashoka to the Buddha.
sections.rise:
The political setting was the rise of Magadha under the Nanda dynasty around 350 BCE, followed by Alexander's campaign in the north-west, which he ended in 325 BCE after a mutiny. Alexander assigned the Indus Valley territories to Greek governors and died in 323 BCE. According to Greek and Roman texts, Chandragupta then attacked the governors during a period of unrest and local warfare and took control of the eastern Indus Valley. Justin writes that Alexander's prefects had been assassinated and that Chandragupta, the author of this liberation, himself oppressed the people he had freed after taking the throne. Justin also says he offended the Nanda king, who ordered his execution, and that he saved himself by flight; he adds omens, a lion that licked the sleeping Chandragupta and a wild elephant that offered itself as his steed.

The Sanskrit play Mudrarakshasa, composed probably between 300 and 700 CE, and Buddhist and Jain legends bring in Chanakya, a Brahmin counsellor who in some versions was insulted by the Nanda king and swore to destroy him. In the Jain account by Hemachandra, written nearly 1,400 years after Chandragupta's death, the army was raised with coins Chanakya minted. Hindu and Jain texts say the war with the Nandas was bitterly fought; Buddhist accounts describe an easy victory. The Nanda king was defeated and exiled in some accounts and killed in the Buddhist ones. Historically reliable details of the campaign are unavailable.
sections.deeds:
The conquest of Magadha is generally dated to c. 322–319 BCE and his expansion into the Punjab to c. 317–312 BCE. Some scholars have suggested that he first built his power in the Punjab, and an alternative chronology based on Justin puts it all in c. 311–305 BCE. Between 305 and 303 BCE Seleucus I Nicator, who had founded the Seleucid Empire in 312 BCE, tried to retake the former satrapies on the Indus. The two formed a dynastic marriage alliance. Strabo, writing about 300 years later, says Seleucus gave the Indus lands to Sandrocottus on terms of intermarriage and in exchange for 500 elephants. The extent of the land is unknown; a modest reading limits it to the western Indus Valley, the Punjab and eastern Gandhara, and scholars such as Coningham and Young question control of eastern Afghanistan and the lower Indus. Seleucus sent Megasthenes as ambassador, who stayed four years. Rudradaman's inscription at Junagadh, about 150 CE, shows Chandragupta's rule reached Gujarat, where his governor Vaishya Pushyagupta had the Sudarshana lake built.

The administration was decentralised, with provinces, local governments and a council of advisers. According to Megasthenes, three bodies handled villages, cities and the military. Chandragupta is credited with irrigation works and roads, including a highway from Pataliputra to Taxila described by Megasthenes. Most scholars now think the Arthashastra is not of Mauryan origin.
sections.opponents:
Accounts of Chandragupta come mostly from sources with their own aims. The Brahmanical Puranas, from Gupta times, viewed the Nandas and Mauryas as illegitimate rulers because of their shudra background. Justin, a Roman writer of the 2nd century CE, accuses Chandragupta of turning the liberation of the Indus peoples into servitude. Plutarch calls him a great king, but not as great in power and influence as Porus or Agrammes, the Greek name for Dhana Nanda.

The Jain accounts hold the conquests responsible for suffering. In the Digambara legend the monk Bhadrabahu foretold a twelve-year famine because of the killing and violence of Chandragupta's conquests, and led monks south. In Hemachandra's Svetambara legend Chandragupta followed non-Jain ascetics with "the wrong view of religion" and lusted for women for fifteen years before Chanakya persuaded him to turn to Jainism; the legend also has Chanakya use violence and cunning to expand the empire and raise revenue. Contemporary Greek evidence says he drank wine, performed Vedic sacrifices and animal sacrifices and enjoyed hunting, which does not suit Jain non-violence. The Arthashastra's prescriptions are incompatible with his reign and that Chanakya's identification with Kautilya dates from a later period.
sections.last:
No ancient text gives the end of his reign. According to some Hindu and Buddhist texts he ruled 24 years. Buddhist sources place his reign 162 years after the Buddha's death, a chronology that differs greatly from the Greek and Roman record, and Jain sources give differing gaps after Mahavira's death. Historians give different dates for the reign: Irfan Habib and Vivekanand Jha c. 322–298 BCE, Upinder Singh 324 or 321 to 297 BCE and Kristi Wiley 320 to 293 BCE. According to Roy, he abdicated c. 298 BCE and died between 297 and 293 BCE.

The Digambara Jain tradition says he gave up his empire to his son Bindusara and joined Bhadrabahu as a monk. They went to Shravanabelagola in present-day Karnataka, where he lived as an ascetic for several years and then fasted to death in the ritual of sallekhana. The tradition is recorded in texts from the 10th century onward, and Jain inscriptions from the 7th to 15th centuries name Bhadrabahu and a Prabhacandra whom later tradition identified as Chandragupta. The doubts are several: the Svetambara texts place Bhadrabahu near the Himalayan foothills, one Digambara version has Samprati Chandragupta, a later Maurya, perform the ritual, and Sushma Jansari concludes that the story developed after about 600 CE.
sections.legacy:
Chandragupta's empire, which reached its peak under his grandson Ashoka, began an era of economic prosperity, reforms and infrastructure expansion. Under his dynasty Buddhism, Jainism and Ajivika gained prominence beside other traditions. After his reign, Seleucus's ambassador Megasthenes left an account of his court, and Greek and Roman authors who quoted it are among the main sources on him. Without them, according to Mookerji, this period would be "a most obscure chapter of Indian history".

The identification proposed by William Jones in 1793 made the dating of early Indian history possible, and his reign has been called "the sheet anchor of Indian chronology". It is uncertain whether his rule reached southern India, since the empire stretched to Karnataka by the time Ashoka took the throne in c. 268 BCE and the conquests may be his or Bindusara's. Sushma Jansari notes that views diverged in the 20th century: western academics tend to take a reserved view of his accomplishments, while Indian authors have portrayed him as a very successful king who established the first Indian nation. A memorial to him stands on Chandragiri hill in Shravanabelagola, and he has been the subject of Sanskrit and Bengali plays and later films and television series.

summary: Chandragupta Maurya (reigned c. 320 – c. 298 BCE) founded the Maurya Empire after defeating the Nanda dynasty and taking the eastern Indus Valley, and formed an alliance with Seleucus I Nicator. His life is known only from late and partisan Greek, Hindu, Buddhist and Jain sources, which disagree on his origins and death.
references: Radhakumud Mookerji, Chandragupta Maurya and His Times (Motilal Banarsidass, 1966)
V. R. Ramachandra Dikshitar, The Mauryan Polity (Motilal Banarsidass, 1993)
notes: Birth year unknown: start is -320, the conventional start of his reign (article: reigned c. 320 BCE – c. 298 BCE), with circa true; born fact says so. End -298 is Roy's abdication date; the article says death was between 297 and 293 BCE and is disputed (endCirca true).
Reign dates vary: the lede 320-298; Habib and Jha 322-298; Singh 324 or 321 to 297; Wiley 320-293; Jansari's later chronology c. 311-305 for the rise. All given as attributed.

The article contradicts itself or is garbled in places: Parishishtaparvan is called both 'Digambara' (lede of the section) and 'Svetambara' (Hemachandra's legend later); I wrote 'the Jain account by Hemachandra' and 'Hemachandra's Svetambara legend' in the opponents section; the Digambara legend of Bhadrabahu's famine is attributed to Digambara accounts only.

The Brhatkathakosa date: 931 CE in one place and 'about the 10th-century' elsewhere; I wrote '10th century onward'. 'Jain legends that developed about 900 years later' (Religion section) versus 'nearly 1,400 years' for Hemachandra left both unused except the 1,400 figure.
Justin: 'Nandrum' vs 'Alexandrum' dispute (a passage once read as a meeting with Alexander) left out; the Plutarch claim is reported as Plutarch's.

Conflicting statement on the defeat of the Greeks: Mookerji 323 BCE, Jansari c. 317; the article's war order (Punjab before or after Magadha) is stated as uncertain. The 323 event in 'ev' is Alexander's death only.
Strabo's date: 'about 300 years after' his death, as the article says; the article's Justin source (ruler 'when Seleucus was laying the foundations') used in the alternative chronology.

Left out: the Tamil Sangam poems, Sisikottus identification, Didarganj Yakshi, the Arthashastra's methods of protection, the Nanda king's daughter marriage (Jain legend), Durdhara, Samprati as 'Jain Ashoka', popular culture and the 2001 stamp.

The Seleucid marriage: the article says the details are unknown and offers several readings (Chandragupta or Bindusara marrying a Seleucid princess; the Rajavamsa and Bhavishya Purana give a daughter of Seleucus); only the alliance is stated.
